title: CLSA Holds Course on TCS, Infosys, HCLTech as Nifty IT Slides Third Day
excerpt: The brokerage warned that cautious demand commentary, geopolitics, higher interest rates and inflation could weigh on Indian IT earnings, as the Nifty IT index fell for a third straight session.
body:
• CLSA retained Hold ratings on TCS, Infosys and HCLTech and Underperform on Wipro, warning that weak demand could weigh on earnings.
  • The Nifty IT index fell 1.5% for a third straight session, with LTIMindtree, HCLTech and Mphasis leading the declines.
  • The brokerage cited cautious demand commentary, geopolitics, higher interest rates and inflation as headwinds for the sector.
  • The call extends a cautious stance from August, when CLSA downgraded TCS, Infosys and Tech Mahindra to Hold over limited upside.

CLSA is staying cautious on India's IT giants. The international brokerage retained its Hold ratings on Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys and HCLTech, and Underperform on Wipro, warning that cautious demand commentary, geopolitics, higher interest rates and inflation could weigh on earnings — as the Nifty IT index slid 1.5% for a third consecutive session, with LTIMindtree, HCLTech and Mphasis leading the losses.

The note lands at a fragile moment for the sector. Indian IT stocks have spent 2026 whipsawed between AI-disruption fears and bargain hunting, and CLSA's latest commentary suggests the brokerage sees the near-term risk skewed to the downside even as valuations have reset.

Weak demand, macro headwinds

CLSA's concern centres on demand. Client discretionary spending remains restrained, and the brokerage flagged a familiar list of drags: cautious commentary from management teams, geopolitical uncertainty, elevated interest rates and persistent inflation. Together, they make for a difficult backdrop for a sector that earns a large share of its revenue from the United States, where enterprise technology budgets are set.

The immediate market reaction was unforgiving. The Nifty IT index's three-day slide underscores how quickly sentiment turns when a major brokerage questions the earnings trajectory — particularly in a year when every IT rally has been met by a fresh round of AI-related selling.

A cautious stance, months in the making

The Hold ratings are not new. In August, CLSA downgraded TCS, Infosys and Tech Mahindra to Hold, cut Wipro and Mphasis to Underperform, and named Persistent Systems and Coforge its high-conviction picks. The rationale then: Q1 earnings were a mixed bag across Indian IT and its global peers, and the large caps offered limited upside after accounting for structural pressures.

CLSA's longer-term view is more constructive. The brokerage has argued that AI volumes could eventually supersede the deflation AI brings to pricing, taking US dollar revenue growth from low to mid-single digits by FY30. The catch is the path there: a long gestation period in which productivity gains compress pricing before AI-led demand scales up.

"Basic Excel maths suggests that AI volumes could supersede deflation by FY30, taking US dollar revenue growth from low to mid-single digits."

— CLSA

An industry arguing with itself over AI

The sector has been the market's favourite battleground this year. Breakthroughs by AI startups earlier in the year triggered a sharp sell-off on fears that the traditional offshore services model could be disrupted. Jefferies downgraded six Indian IT companies in February, cutting TCS to underperform and Infosys and HCLTech to hold, arguing the stocks offered more downside than upside even after the correction.

Other brokerages have pushed back. HSBC called India an "anti-AI" diversifier, arguing AI-rotation outflows from the country had largely played out, while Morgan Stanley has pointed to largecaps such as Infosys and TCS as beneficiaries of a relief rally ahead of earnings season. CLSA itself noted in a separate commentary that it sees no AI-led pricing pressure in deal renewals yet, though client decision-making is slowing amid AI-related shifts.

The one point of agreement: valuations have corrected to roughly their 10-year average, making the sector cheaper than it has been in years — the debate is entirely about whether earnings can grow into them.

What to watch

The next data points are the Q2 earnings calls, where management commentary on deal pipelines and client budgets will either validate CLSA's caution or undercut it. Investors will also be watching US Federal Reserve policy and the trajectory of enterprise spending into 2027. For now, CLSA's message is clear: the large caps are fairly valued, the mid-tier AI plays carry the momentum, and patience — not chasing — is the trade.
nri_angle: Indian IT stocks are core holdings for many diaspora portfolios, and CLSA's sustained Hold stance signals the large caps may stay range-bound until earnings reaccelerate.
